body:
Background to Muslim Reform Movements

The nineteenth century saw important religious, educational and social movements among Indian Muslims. These movements developed under changing political and economic circumstances, but they did not share a single programme or political outlook.

The decline of Mughal political authority, expansion of British rule, changes in administration and the growth of Western education created new challenges for established institutions.

After the Revolt of 1857, the ending of Company rule and the consolidation of British Crown rule intensified debates about the future of Muslim education, religious learning and participation in public affairs.

The responses differed according to region, social background, religious understanding and political priorities.

Different Understandings of Reform

Some Muslim reformers considered modern education essential for overcoming social and economic disadvantages. Others argued that the urgent task was to preserve Islamic learning and strengthen religious practice. Still others concentrated on religious interpretation, preaching or the problems of rural communities.

These approaches produced several important movements.

  • Aligarh Movement: Emphasized modern education, English and Western science while maintaining Muslim cultural and religious identity.
  • Deoband Movement: Emphasized systematic Islamic religious education and the preservation and renewal of Islamic scholarship.
  • Ahmadiyya Movement: Developed around the religious claims and teachings of Mirza Ghulam Ahmad and became known for missionary activity and public religious debate.
  • Faraizi and related revivalist movements: Emphasized religious obligations and, in some regions, became connected with agrarian grievances.
  • Barelvi and other theological currents: Developed distinctive interpretations of Islamic tradition, devotion and religious authority.

These categories describe their principal historical emphasis, not the complete range of activities undertaken by every follower.

The Importance of Education

Education was central to many reform movements, but the meaning of educational improvement varied.

For reformers associated with Aligarh, the ability to study modern science and English was necessary for access to new occupations and public institutions.

For the scholars associated with Deoband, the preservation of knowledge of the Quran, Hadith, Islamic jurisprudence and related disciplines was essential for maintaining religious life under colonial conditions.

Both movements valued education, but their educational priorities and institutional models were different.

Printing and Public Religious Debate

The expansion of printing, especially inexpensive lithographic printing, made religious and educational literature more accessible.

Scholars published books, translations, pamphlets and newspapers in languages including Urdu and Persian. These publications allowed religious disagreements to reach a much wider audience.

Muslim religious scholars, known as ulama, used printed works to explain Islamic teachings and respond to religious controversies.

Fatwa

A fatwa is a legal opinion concerning an issue of Islamic law, issued by a qualified religious scholar such as a mufti. It provides religious-legal guidance and is not automatically equivalent to an enforceable judgment of a state court.

The Deoband seminary became particularly associated with the production and circulation of fatwas dealing with religious doctrine and questions of everyday conduct.

Religious Reform and Political Diversity

Religious reform did not lead every Muslim intellectual or organization towards the same political position.

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan encouraged cooperation with colonial authorities and was critical of the early Indian National Congress. By contrast, several scholars associated with the Deoband tradition participated in anti-colonial political movements.

Other religious groups concentrated mainly on preaching, theological disagreements or social reform.

Therefore, an institution's theological position and its political activity must be identified separately. A shared religious identity does not establish a shared political programme.

Prelims focus

  • The major Muslim reform movements followed different educational, theological and political approaches.
  • Aligarh: Modern education and scientific learning.
  • Deoband: Islamic religious scholarship and education.
  • Ahmadiyya: Distinct religious claims, preaching and religious debate.
  • Ulama: Scholars of Islamic religious learning and law.
  • Fatwa: A scholarly opinion on Islamic law.
  • Trap: Muslim reform movements should not be treated as a single organization or as followers of one common political ideology.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, printed pp. 98 and 107; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, section 7, Religious Reform and Public Debates, printed pp. 169–170; Aligarh Muslim University, History; Banglapedia, Muslim Religious Movements. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Muslim Reform in Colonial India: Historical Context, Education and Religious Debate

body:
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817–1898)

The Aligarh Movement was a major nineteenth-century movement for educational, intellectual and social improvement among Indian Muslims.

Its principal leader was Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, born in Delhi on 17 October 1817. He worked in the judicial and administrative system under British rule and lived through the Revolt of 1857.

The events of 1857 influenced his assessment of Muslim society's political and educational position.

Sir Syed believed that acquiring English education, modern scientific knowledge and access to new professions was essential for the advancement of Muslims under the changing colonial administration.

His educational programme sought to combine modern knowledge with the preservation of Muslim religious and cultural identity.

The Scientific Society and Educational Reform

Sir Syed established the Scientific Society in 1864 to encourage scientific learning and make useful Western knowledge available through translation into Indian languages.

The Society sought to make modern ideas accessible to people who did not necessarily read English. Translation, publication and discussion therefore formed important parts of the Aligarh Movement.

The Aligarh Institute Gazette, launched in 1866, helped circulate educational and intellectual discussions.

Sir Syed also founded the reform periodical Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq in 1870. It promoted discussion of education, ethics, social conduct and reform.

These activities demonstrate that the Aligarh Movement was broader than a single college. It included publication, translation, institutional development and efforts to encourage changes in social attitudes.

From the Aligarh School to Aligarh Muslim University

The educational institution associated with the movement developed in stages.

  • 1875: The Madarsatul Uloom school was established at Aligarh.
  • 1877: The Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, commonly called MAO College, was formally established.
  • 1886: Sir Syed established the All India Muhammadan Educational Conference to encourage educational development beyond Aligarh.
  • 1920: The college was transformed into Aligarh Muslim University (AMU).

The college adopted elements of the educational model of English universities while retaining a place for Islamic learning and Muslim cultural life.

Its importance lay partly in producing an educated class prepared to participate in professional, administrative, intellectual and public life.

Distinguishing the institutional dates

The NCERT Class 8 account associates the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental institution with 1875. Aligarh Muslim University's detailed institutional history distinguishes the 1875 school from the 1877 college. The university was created in 1920. These dates describe stages of the same institutional development.

Religious Thought and Scientific Knowledge

Sir Syed also attempted to reconcile Islamic religious understanding with modern scientific knowledge.

He argued that religious interpretation should take account of reason and knowledge of the natural world. His approach encouraged reconsideration of certain inherited interpretations in the light of modern learning.

Such views were controversial among some traditional religious scholars. Nevertheless, Sir Syed did not advocate abandoning Islam; his objective was to show that Islamic faith and modern intellectual development could coexist.

This approach is commonly described as Muslim modernism.

Political Outlook of the Aligarh Movement

Sir Syed's political position developed partly from his concern that Muslims required educational and economic advancement before entering unfamiliar forms of representative politics.

He encouraged cooperation with the British administration and was critical of the early Indian National Congress, established in 1885.

He feared that political representation based mainly on numerical majorities could disadvantage Muslims in some circumstances.

His approach therefore emphasized education, community advancement and political caution rather than immediate mass anti-colonial agitation.

Sir Syed's opposition to the early Congress should not be presented as the position of every Indian Muslim. Muslim political opinion was diverse, and members of the Muslim community participated in several different political and nationalist movements.

The Aligarh Movement also should not be confused with the All India Muslim League, which was founded later, in 1906 at Dacca. The Aligarh Movement was primarily an educational and intellectual reform movement, whereas the Muslim League was a political organization.

Women and Educational Reform

The wider process of educational reform among Muslims also involved women and women-led initiatives.

The Begums of Bhopal supported educational development and became important patrons of Muslim education. They were associated with efforts to promote girls' education, including a primary school for girls at Aligarh.

Other reformers, such as Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, worked to expand education among Muslim girls in eastern India.

These activities were part of broader Muslim social and educational reform and should not all be treated as institutions directly founded by Sir Syed.

Prelims focus

  • Sir Syed Ahmad Khan: 1817–1898; principal leader of the Aligarh Movement.
  • Scientific Society: 1864; translation and dissemination of scientific knowledge.
  • Aligarh Institute Gazette: 1866.
  • Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq: 1870; social and intellectual reform periodical.
  • Aligarh school: 1875; MAO College: 1877; AMU: 1920.
  • Muhammadan Educational Conference: 1886.
  • Trap: The Aligarh Movement, MAO College, AMU and the All India Muslim League are not interchangeable names for one organization.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, printed pp. 98 and 107; Aligarh Muslim University, History, institutional chronology; Aligarh Muslim University, The Founder; Aligarh Muslim University, Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq, Brief Introduction; Aligarh Muslim University, Maulana Azad Library, About the Library, section Sir Syed; S. Irfan Habib, Reconciling Science with Islam in 19th Century India, Indian Economic and Social History Review, vol. 34, issue 1, abstract. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Aligarh Movement: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, Modern Education and Politics

body:
Origins of the Deoband Movement

The Deoband Movement was an influential movement of Islamic religious education and reform that developed in northern India during the nineteenth century.

Its principal institutional centre was Darul Uloom Deoband, a religious seminary established at Deoband in present-day Uttar Pradesh, in the district of Saharanpur.

The movement emerged in the setting of declining older political institutions, the consequences of the Revolt of 1857 and the expansion of British colonial administration.

Religious scholars feared that traditional systems of Islamic education would weaken under these circumstances. Their response was to establish an organized institution for the teaching and preservation of Islamic scholarship.

Foundation and Leading Personalities

The establishment of Darul Uloom Deoband is generally dated to 1866 in the institution's own historical accounts.

Its principal founder was Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi. Other important figures associated with its early development included Rashid Ahmad Gangohi and Haji Abid Husain.

The seminary developed a system of religious instruction that became influential far beyond Deoband itself.

Why 1866 and 1867 both appear

Institutional histories of Darul Uloom Deoband place its foundation in 1866. The NCERT Class 10 chapter on print culture gives the founding year as 1867. These references concern the same seminary, not 2 separate institutions. The difference should be retained when interpreting textbook-based chronology questions.

Educational and Religious Objectives

The Deoband institution concentrated on the study of Islamic religious sciences.

Its curriculum emphasized subjects such as the Quran, Hadith, Islamic jurisprudence, Arabic and traditional religious scholarship.

Hadith refers to reports concerning the sayings, actions and approvals of Prophet Muhammad. Fiqh means Islamic jurisprudence, or the scholarly understanding and application of Islamic legal principles.

The Deoband tradition developed principally within Sunni Hanafi Islamic scholarship. The Hanafi school is one of the major schools of Sunni Islamic jurisprudence.

The movement emphasized the authority of religious learning, disciplined religious practice and reform of customs that its scholars considered inconsistent with Islamic teachings.

Its founders sought to maintain a strong network of educated religious scholars who could teach and guide Muslim communities.

Deoband and Modern Education

The difference between Deoband and Aligarh was primarily one of educational priority and intellectual approach.

Aligarh placed major emphasis on English education, Western scientific learning and preparation for modern professions.

Deoband concentrated on the systematic preservation and transmission of Islamic religious knowledge.

Deoband's emphasis on religious scholarship should not be simplified into a claim that every Deobandi scholar rejected every form of modern knowledge or technology. The comparison concerns the movements' principal institutional purposes.

Print Culture and the Circulation of Fatwas

The Deoband Movement made extensive use of printed religious literature.

Urdu publications and printed fatwas helped scholars communicate interpretations of Islamic law and religious conduct to people who could not attend the seminary.

For example, a person might seek guidance about a question of everyday religious practice. A qualified scholar could issue a fatwa explaining the relevant religious-legal interpretation. Printing allowed such opinions to circulate among a larger readership.

Thus, the movement combined traditional religious scholarship with an expanding modern print network.

Political Developments and the Freedom Movement

Several scholars associated with the Deoband tradition participated in anti-colonial politics. Their activities should be distinguished from the educational functions of the seminary itself.

An important later development was the establishment of Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind in 1919.

The organization included prominent religious scholars and participated in anti-colonial political activity. It supported forms of cooperation with the wider nationalist movement, including the Non-Cooperation Movement.

Its political outlook included the idea that Muslims and non-Muslims could cooperate in a common struggle against colonial rule.

This differed from Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's earlier preference for cooperation with the British authorities and his criticism of the early Congress.

Deoband was primarily a religious educational movement. Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind, established in 1919, was a separate organization associated with the political activities of many religious scholars. They should not be treated as the same institution.

Historical Significance

The Deoband Movement helped preserve and extend Islamic religious scholarship in colonial India.

Its network of teachers, students, seminaries and publications influenced religious education across different regions of South Asia.

Its history also demonstrates that religious education and political nationalism were not necessarily opposed. Some scholars regarded the defence of religious and community interests as compatible with participation in the struggle against colonial rule.

Prelims focus

  • Institution: Darul Uloom Deoband.
  • Place: Deoband, Saharanpur district, present-day Uttar Pradesh.
  • Foundation: 1866 in institutional histories; 1867 in the NCERT Class 10 account.
  • Leading figures: Muhammad Qasim Nanautavi and Rashid Ahmad Gangohi.
  • Educational emphasis: Quran, Hadith, jurisprudence and Islamic religious scholarship.
  • Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind: Founded in 1919; associated with anti-colonial political activity.
  • Trap: Deoband should not be matched with Sir Syed Ahmad Khan or the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College.

[Sources: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter Print Culture and the Modern World, section 7, printed p. 169; Darul Uloom Waqf Deoband, institutional introduction and history of the founder; Darul Uloom Deoband, Dar al-Ulum Deoband: A Brief Account of Its Establishment and Background, section Founding of Dar al-Ulum; Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind, History and Founders, sections Establishment in 1919 and Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Deoband Movement: Islamic Scholarship, Religious Education and Nationalist Politics
